resources.title: American coot
resources.description: Identify American coot, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: American coot (Fulica americana): About 15 in (38 cm); charcoal gray body with a blacker head. Thick white bill with a white and chestnut frontal shield running up the forehead. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Occurs across much of Canada and the United States, from western and eastern Canada south through all U.S. regions; northern birds migrate and may winter wherever water stays open.

rangeSummary.value: Occurs across much of Canada and the United States, from western and eastern Canada south through all U.S. regions; northern birds migrate and may winter wherever water stays open.

identification.text: About 15 in (38 cm); charcoal gray body with a blacker head.
Thick white bill with a white and chestnut frontal shield running up the forehead.
Big feet with lobed (not webbed) toes, visible when it walks on land.
Nods its head as it swims.
Immatures are paler gray; downy young have a red head.

habitat.text: Ponds, lakes and marshes; breeds on fairly shallow fresh water with much marsh vegetation.
In winter also on park ponds, reservoirs, fields near water, salt marshes and protected coastal bays.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Usually in flocks; aggressive and noisy, calling day or night with clucks, cackles and grunts.
Must patter across the water, flapping hard, to take off.
Feeds by dabbling, up-ending, diving and grazing on land; steals food from ducks. Diet mostly aquatic plants and algae plus insects, snails and other small animals.
Some populations are resident, others migrate, probably mostly at night; may winter as far north as open water allows.

resources.title: American crow
resources.description: Identify American crow, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: American crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos): Entirely black, 41–53 cm long, with a strong bill. Relatively short, square-tipped tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from coastal and southeastern Alaska and across southern and central Canada (north to the southwestern Northwest Territories, northern Prairie Provinces, northern Ontario, south-central Quebec and Newfoundland) south through most of the United States to the Gulf coast and southern Florida.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from coastal and southeastern Alaska and across southern and central Canada (north to the southwestern Northwest Territories, northern Prairie Provinces, northern Ontario, south-central Quebec and Newfoundland) south through most of the United States to the Gulf coast and southern Florida.

identification.text: Entirely black, 41–53 cm long, with a strong bill.
Relatively short, square-tipped tail.
Sexes look alike.
Voice is the familiar falling caw-caw or caa-caa.
Compared with the blackbirds (icteridae): Blackbirds are all smaller than the crow, with different voices and shapes.

habitat.text: Semi-open country: farmland, fields, woodland clearings, river groves, shores, towns and city parks; avoids hot desert.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Sociable outside nesting; gathers in communal winter night roosts that can hold thousands of birds
Feeds mostly on the ground; omnivorous, scavenging roads and dumps and taking insects, grain, carrion, eggs and nestlings
Drops hard-shelled mollusks from height onto rocks and coughs up pellets of indigestible food
Resident in many areas; birds breeding north of southern Canada move south for winter

resources.title: Band-tailed pigeon
resources.description: Identify Band-tailed pigeon, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Band-tailed pigeon (Patagioenas fasciata): Large pigeon, 35-40 cm, bigger than the familiar park pigeon. Narrow white band across the nape (absent on juveniles) above green iridescence on the neck. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Western North America, from Western Canada and the Pacific Coast south through California, the Rocky Mountains, the Southwest and Texas. Present year-round in parts of the Pacific Coast; mainly a summer resident elsewhere.

rangeSummary.value: Western North America, from Western Canada and the Pacific Coast south through California, the Rocky Mountains, the Southwest and Texas. Present year-round in parts of the Pacific Coast; mainly a summer resident elsewhere.

identification.text: Large pigeon, 35-40 cm, bigger than the familiar park pigeon.
Narrow white band across the nape (absent on juveniles) above green iridescence on the neck.
Yellow base to the bill.
Wide grey band across the tail.
Purplish-pink head and chest; sexes similar.
Compared with the rock pigeon: The band-tailed pigeon is larger, with a white nape band, yellow-based bill and wide grey tail band.

habitat.text: Oak canyons, foothills, chaparral and mountain forests, including pine-oak and fir forest. Increasingly regular in suburban areas on the Pacific Coast.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Sociable; forages in flocks in most seasons, even during breeding, and often nests in small loose colonies.
Nomadic, concentrating where acorns, berries and other wild food crops are abundant.
Feeds both on the ground and in trees, clambering in small branches and even hanging upside down for berries.
Diet is dominated by acorns when available, plus berries such as elderberry, manzanita, juniper and wild grape.

resources.title: Black scoter
resources.description: Identify Black scoter, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Black scoter (Melanitta americana): Adult drake is entirely black except for an orange knob on the bill. Hens and young drakes are dark with a contrasting pale face and foreneck. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds in Alaska and northern Canada; winters along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and occurs on the Great Lakes in migration.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds in Alaska and northern Canada; winters along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and occurs on the Great Lakes in migration.

identification.text: Adult drake is entirely black except for an orange knob on the bill.
Hens and young drakes are dark with a contrasting pale face and foreneck.
Crow-sized sea duck; floats buoyantly with the tail often cocked up.
Compared with the ruddy duck: A winter drake ruddy duck is smaller and paler with a relatively larger bill.

habitat.text: Breeds on coastal and wet tundra and tundra openings in northern forest. Winters on bays and exposed coasts over shallow water, mostly within a mile of shore; uses the Great Lakes in migration.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: More vocal than other scoters; in spring gives a musical whistled cour-loo.
Dives for mussels and other bivalves, crustaceans and marine worms at sea; eats aquatic insects, fish eggs and plants on summer fresh water.
Migrates early in spring and late in fall; coastal flocks fly low offshore.

resources.title: Cinnamon teal
resources.description: Identify Cinnamon teal, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Cinnamon teal (Spatula cyanoptera): Breeding male: bright chestnut (cinnamon) body and head with red eyes. Female: very like a female blue-winged teal with the same wing pattern, but with a slightly heavier, longer bill and a plainer, browner face. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Strictly western in North America: breeds and occurs mainly from Western Canada south through the Northwest, Rocky Mountains, Plains, California, the Southwest and Texas, with scattered records farther east. Also has nesting populations in South America.

rangeSummary.value: Strictly western in North America: breeds and occurs mainly from Western Canada south through the Northwest, Rocky Mountains, Plains, California, the Southwest and Texas, with scattered records farther east. Also has nesting populations in South America.

identification.text: Breeding male: bright chestnut (cinnamon) body and head with red eyes.
Female: very like a female blue-winged teal with the same wing pattern, but with a slightly heavier, longer bill and a plainer, browner face.
Males in fall eclipse plumage look much like females except for their red eyes.
Small dabbling duck, 36-41 cm.
Compared with the blue-winged teal: Females share the same wing pattern; the cinnamon teal female has a longer, heavier bill and a plainer, browner face.

habitat.text: Freshwater marshes and fresh or alkaline shallow lakes with extensive marsh; generally not coastal salt marsh. In migration may stop on any small pond or reservoir.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Forages in shallow water swimming forward with head partly submerged, straining food; one bird often follows another to feed on food stirred up.
Eats mainly plant seeds (smartweeds, sedges, grasses, pondweeds) plus insects, snails and small crustaceans.
A shorter-distance migrant than the blue-winged teal; may migrate mostly by day.

resources.title: Common eider
resources.description: Identify Common eider, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Common eider (Somateria mollissima): Large, heavy-bodied sea duck: 23-30 in, among the biggest ducks. Adult male distinctive black-and-white; bill color varies from orange (Alaska) to olive-gray (Northeast). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds along northern coasts of Alaska and Canada, including Hudson Bay and the Atlantic coast; the winter range extends only a little south of the breeding range, reaching New England and the Mid-Atlantic.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds along northern coasts of Alaska and Canada, including Hudson Bay and the Atlantic coast; the winter range extends only a little south of the breeding range, reaching New England and the Mid-Atlantic.

identification.text: Large, heavy-bodied sea duck: 23-30 in, among the biggest ducks.
Adult male distinctive black-and-white; bill color varies from orange (Alaska) to olive-gray (Northeast).
Female: large, with a long sloping bill and heavy barring on the sides; grayish to rusty brown.
Young males pass through dark-headed, white-chested stages.

habitat.text: Stays very close to coastlines in all seasons: rocky coasts and shoals, and in summer islands and coastal tundra.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Floats offshore in flocks that can number several thousand; often nests in colonies.
Dives mainly for mussels and other bivalves, also crabs and other invertebrates; often feeds on falling or low tide, by day or night.
Northernmost breeders migrate long distances; southern breeders are more sedentary; Hudson Bay birds stay all year in open leads.
Male courtship calls are a hollow moan and cooing notes; female quacks.

resources.title: Common gallinule
resources.description: Identify Common gallinule, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Common gallinule (Gallinula galeata): Slaty body with a browner back and a white stripe along the side. Thick bill and frontal shield usually red and yellow (sometimes all yellow or brownish). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from central California, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, southern Wisconsin, southern Ontario, New England and Nova Scotia south through Central and South America. In eastern North America it winters mainly from South Carolina and the Gulf Coast south.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from central California, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, southern Wisconsin, southern Ontario, New England and Nova Scotia south through Central and South America. In eastern North America it winters mainly from South Carolina and the Gulf Coast south.

identification.text: Slaty body with a browner back and a white stripe along the side.
Thick bill and frontal shield usually red and yellow (sometimes all yellow or brownish).
Greenish legs.
Immature is paler gray with dull bill and legs but still shows the white side stripe.
Compared with the american coot: Often found together; the gallinule shows a white side stripe and red-and-yellow bill shield and keeps closer to dense marsh cover.

habitat.text: Fresh marshes and reedy ponds with still or slow water, some open water and dense cover along the margins.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Swims buoyantly, bobbing its head; also walks on open ground and clambers through reeds and cattails
Feeds on water-plant leaves, stems and seeds plus insects, snails and tadpoles; may up-end or dive
Gives squawking and croaking notes similar to the American coot
Northern populations migrate (probably at night), arriving in April and leaving by October; southern populations are largely resident

conservationStatus.text: Hawaiian common gallinule (Gallinula galeata sandvicensis): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.

resources.title: Common merganser
resources.description: Identify Common merganser, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Common merganser (Mergus merganser): Drake: mostly white body, black back and iridescent green head. Red bill, thick at the base and narrowing to the tip. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds across Alaska and Canada and occurs through most of the continental US in suitable habitat.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds across Alaska and Canada and occurs through most of the continental US in suitable habitat.

identification.text: Drake: mostly white body, black back and iridescent green head.
Red bill, thick at the base and narrowing to the tip.
Hen: gray body with a bright rusty head and a sharply defined white throat.
Compared with the red-breasted merganser: Hens are similar; compare the common merganser hen's sharply defined white throat.
Compared with the mallard: Other green-headed ducks such as the mallard have a different body pattern and shape.

habitat.text: Clear rivers and lakes in forested country in summer; lakes, large rivers and occasionally coastal bays in winter. Mainly fresh water.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Dives and swims underwater, kicking both feet together; hunts mostly by sight.
Eats mainly fish, also mussels, shrimp and salamanders.
Gives low rasping croaks.
Migrates late in fall and early in spring; males winter farther north than females and young.

resources.title: Eurasian collared-dove
resources.description: Identify Eurasian collared-dove, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Eurasian collared-dove (Streptopelia decaocto): 11.4-12.6 in; pale brown-gray dove with a narrow black ring on the back of the neck. Big white patches in the outer tail feathers; tail squared or slightly rounded. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Introduced: reached the Bahamas in 1974, then Florida, and has since spread west and north across much of North America to Oregon and Washington; the Northeast has only scattered strays.

rangeSummary.value: Introduced: reached the Bahamas in 1974, then Florida, and has since spread west and north across much of North America to Oregon and Washington; the Northeast has only scattered strays.

identification.text: 11.4-12.6 in; pale brown-gray dove with a narrow black ring on the back of the neck.
Big white patches in the outer tail feathers; tail squared or slightly rounded.
Call a deep, repeated 'kuk-KOOOO-kuk'; also a harsh, mewing nasal note.
Compared with the mourning dove: Look for the collared-dove's narrow black neck ring and big white patches in the squared outer tail.

habitat.text: Residential areas and farmland with a mix of trees and open ground; thrives better in small towns than large cities.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Forages mostly while walking on the ground, in flocks outside the breeding season; eats mainly seeds and waste grain, some berries and insects.
Male display flight: steep climb with noisy wingbeats, then a spiral glide with wings and tail spread.
No regular migration; young birds disperse long distances, driving the species' spread.

resources.title: Fish crow
resources.description: Identify Fish crow, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Fish crow (Corvus ossifragus): All-black crow, 36-41 cm, slightly smaller than the American crow with slightly more pointed wingtips. Identified with certainty only by voice: a nasal 'kwok' and a nasal two-noted 'ah-ah'. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and southeastern United States: Florida, the Southeast, Texas, the Mid-Atlantic and New England, extending up river valleys into the Plains and Great Lakes region.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and southeastern United States: Florida, the Southeast, Texas, the Mid-Atlantic and New England, extending up river valleys into the Plains and Great Lakes region.

identification.text: All-black crow, 36-41 cm, slightly smaller than the American crow with slightly more pointed wingtips.
Identified with certainty only by voice: a nasal 'kwok' and a nasal two-noted 'ah-ah'.
Sexes similar.
Compared with the american crow: The American crow gives a familiar 'caw' rather than a nasal 'kwok' or 'ah-ah', though young American crows also make nasal calls in breeding season.

habitat.text: Tidewater, river valleys, swamps, woodland and farmland, usually nearer water than the American crow, especially beaches, marshes and estuaries.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Mostly a permanent resident; withdraws from some inland parts of its range in winter.
On the coast hunts salt marshes and tidal flats and scavenges on beaches; inland follows swamps and large river drainages.
Often nests in loose colonies of a few pairs.
Has expanded its range farther inland and north, notably on the Atlantic coastal plain and up the Mississippi Valley.

resources.title: Harlequin duck
resources.description: Identify Harlequin duck, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Harlequin duck (Histrionicus histrionicus): 15-17 in; small duck with a short bill. Male: slaty blue with an intricate white pattern and reddish sides. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds in Alaska, western Canada and the northern Rockies and in eastern Canada; winters along the Pacific coast and the North Atlantic coast from eastern Canada to New England and the Mid-Atlantic.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds in Alaska, western Canada and the northern Rockies and in eastern Canada; winters along the Pacific coast and the North Atlantic coast from eastern Canada to New England and the Mid-Atlantic.

identification.text: 15-17 in; small duck with a short bill.
Male: slaty blue with an intricate white pattern and reddish sides.
Female: dark brown with two or three white face spots; smaller and much shorter-billed than scoters.
Call a mouse-like squeak and low whistles.
Compared with the bufflehead (female): Audubon lists female bufflehead and female scaup as comparison species; female harlequin is dark brown with two or three white face spots.
Compared with the scoters (female): Female harlequin looks smaller than a scoter with a much shorter bill.

habitat.text: Nests along shallow, fast-moving rivers and streams, often in forested country, generally not on glacier-fed streams.
Winters on exposed rocky ocean coasts where surf pounds, seldom on sheltered bays.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Swims and dives against the current of rushing rivers and climbs on slippery rocks.
Pairs flying inland follow every bend of the river rather than cutting overland.
Mostly a short-distance migrant from inland nesting streams to nearby coasts.
Feeds by diving and walking on the bottom, prying mollusks and crustaceans off rocks; eats aquatic insects on rivers.

resources.title: Hooded merganser
resources.description: Identify Hooded merganser, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Hooded merganser (Lophodytes cucullatus): Smallest North American merganser, 41–48 cm. Male's crest is white with a black border and can be raised high or flattened. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from southeastern Alaska, central British Columbia and southwestern Alberta south to Oregon, Idaho and Montana, and from central Saskatchewan to Nova Scotia south to Kansas, Louisiana and Georgia; winters mainly along the Pacific, Atlantic and Gulf slopes.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from southeastern Alaska, central British Columbia and southwestern Alberta south to Oregon, Idaho and Montana, and from central Saskatchewan to Nova Scotia south to Kansas, Louisiana and Georgia; winters mainly along the Pacific, Atlantic and Gulf slopes.

identification.text: Smallest North American merganser, 41–48 cm.
Male's crest is white with a black border and can be raised high or flattened.
Female is uniformly dark with a mostly dark bill and a pale bushy crest at the back of a long flat head.
Compared with the bufflehead (male): Compare males closely; the hooded merganser's white crest is bordered with black.

habitat.text: Wooded lakes, ponds, creeks and narrow rivers in forested country; in winter woodland ponds, wooded swamps and fresh or brackish coastal estuaries.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Dives and hunts by sight for small fish, crayfish and aquatic insects
Cavity nester that readily uses wood duck nest boxes
Mostly a short-distance migrant, moving late in fall and early in spring

resources.title: King eider
resources.description: Identify King eider, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: King eider (Somateria spectabilis): Adult male: orange frontal shield on the bill, powder-blue head and much black on the back. Female: brown, much like a female common eider but with a different head shape and a scalloped (not barred) pattern on the sides. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds across the Arctic of Alaska and northern Canada; winters mainly in far northern seas, with small numbers south along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and strays as far as Florida, Louisiana, Kansas and southern California.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds across the Arctic of Alaska and northern Canada; winters mainly in far northern seas, with small numbers south along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and strays as far as Florida, Louisiana, Kansas and southern California.

identification.text: Adult male: orange frontal shield on the bill, powder-blue head and much black on the back.
Female: brown, much like a female common eider but with a different head shape and a scalloped (not barred) pattern on the sides.
Young male: resembles a young male common eider but with a shorter bill and more square-looking head.
Large sea duck, 53-71 cm.
Compared with the common eider: Female king eiders have scalloped, not barred, sides and a different head shape; young males have a shorter bill and squarer head.

habitat.text: Nests on high Arctic tundra, both on the coast and around inland freshwater lakes. Winters on the ocean in the far north, including pack-ice edges; less tied to the coast than the common eider and rare on fresh water such as the Great Lakes.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Forages mainly underwater, often in deep water, diving more than 45 m (150 ft).
Molluscs are a main food at most times, plus crustaceans, echinoderms and insects; insect larvae may dominate in summer.

Spring migration begins very early, with flocks moving north over mostly frozen seas by early April; migrants to the central Canadian Arctic go around Alaska and northeastern Canada rather than overland.

resources.title: King rail
resources.description: Identify King rail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: King rail (Rallus elegans): Large, crow-sized marsh rail. Flanks sharply barred black and white; back feathers edged warm buff; much reddish on the wings. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern North America: eastern Canada and the Great Lakes through New England, the Mid-Atlantic, the Plains and the Southeast to Florida and Texas; withdraws from northern areas in winter.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern North America: eastern Canada and the Great Lakes through New England, the Mid-Atlantic, the Plains and the Southeast to Florida and Texas; withdraws from northern areas in winter.

identification.text: Large, crow-sized marsh rail.
Flanks sharply barred black and white; back feathers edged warm buff; much reddish on the wings.
More richly coloured than the clapper rail.
Compared with the clapper rail: King rail is more richly coloured with sharper black-and-white flank bars; its voice is nearly identical.
Compared with the virginia rail: Virginia rail is much smaller and has gray cheeks.

habitat.text: Fresh and brackish marshes, rice fields and swamps with dense cattail, bulrush or spartina; occasionally salt marsh in winter.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Call is a harsh, clattering kek-kek-kek, almost identical to the clapper rail's.
Forages in shallow water near dense cover; carries large prey such as crayfish to solid ground.
Eats aquatic insects, crayfish, crabs, small fish, snails, frogs and seeds.
Withdraws from northern areas in winter; apparently migrates at night.

resources.title: Long-tailed duck
resources.description: Identify Long-tailed duck, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Long-tailed duck (Clangula hyemalis): Very different summer and winter plumages. Adult male has a long, pointed tail and a strikingly contrasting pattern. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds in Arctic Alaska and northern Canada; winters on northern waters such as the Bering Sea, Hudson Bay and the Great Lakes, and along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts, with scattered inland records across the United States.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds in Arctic Alaska and northern Canada; winters on northern waters such as the Bering Sea, Hudson Bay and the Great Lakes, and along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts, with scattered inland records across the United States.

identification.text: Very different summer and winter plumages.
Adult male has a long, pointed tail and a strikingly contrasting pattern.
Females and young males are paler with less contrast, a squarish head and a stubby bill.
All plumages show solidly dark wings in flight.
Compared with the northern pintail: Audubon notes the male long-tailed duck should be compared with the pintail; the long-tailed duck is a diving sea duck with solidly dark wings in all plumages.

habitat.text: Breeds on low tundra, hilly barren ground and the edges of northern forest near open water. Winters mainly on the ocean, including far offshore among pack ice, and on the Great Lakes and other large fresh waters.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Far more vocal than most ducks; flocks give loud, melodious calls heard at a distance, the male's courtship call a repeated 'ow-owdle-ow'.
Flocks fly low over the sea with stiff, shallow wingbeats, often tilting from side to side.
Dives from the surface propelled mainly by its feet; most feeding is within about 9 m (30 ft) of the surface.
Migrates late in fall and early in spring, often in flocks of hundreds, many following coastlines.

resources.title: Mute swan
resources.description: Identify Mute swan, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Mute swan (Cygnus olor): Very large, all-white swan, 1.4-1.6 m long. Orange bill with a raised black knob at the base. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Introduced from Europe as an ornamental bird and naturalized in North America, mainly in the northeastern United States (including Chesapeake Bay and southern New England) and the Great Lakes, with records in Eastern and Western Canada, the Plains and the Southeast. Native to Eurasia.

rangeSummary.value: Introduced from Europe as an ornamental bird and naturalized in North America, mainly in the northeastern United States (including Chesapeake Bay and southern New England) and the Great Lakes, with records in Eastern and Western Canada, the Plains and the Southeast. Native to Eurasia.

identification.text: Very large, all-white swan, 1.4-1.6 m long.
Orange bill with a raised black knob at the base.
Often swims with its neck in a graceful S-curve, sometimes with wings arched above its back.
Young birds are duller, brownish-grey, with a grey bill.
Compared with the trumpeter swan: The mute swan has an orange bill with a black knob and a quieter, hoarse voice than native swans.
Compared with the tundra swan: The mute swan's orange bill with a black knob separates it from native swans.

habitat.text: Fresh and salt ponds, coastal lagoons, salt bays, marshes, lakes and park ponds, often close to people but also in some remote areas.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Usually silent apart from hissing and barking notes, but its wingbeats make a loud whirring sound audible up to about 1.6 km (a mile) away.
Feeds by dabbling, dipping its head and neck, up-ending and grazing on land; eats aquatic plants such as pondweeds and eelgrass, grass and waste grain.
North American birds move only as far as needed; northeastern birds shift south or to coastal waters when breeding lakes freeze.
Defends nesting areas with wings arched over the back and neck feathers fluffed while swimming forward jerkily.

resources.title: Purple gallinule
resources.description: Identify Purple gallinule, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Purple gallinule (Porphyrio martinicus): 11-14.5 in; adult mostly purple and green with a pale blue frontal shield above a red-and-yellow bill. Bright yellow legs and long toes; white undertail coverts. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds in the southeastern United States and Texas and withdraws in winter mostly to southern Florida; strays wander north as far as Canada at any season.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds in the southeastern United States and Texas and withdraws in winter mostly to southern Florida; strays wander north as far as Canada at any season.

identification.text: 11-14.5 in; adult mostly purple and green with a pale blue frontal shield above a red-and-yellow bill.
Bright yellow legs and long toes; white undertail coverts.
Immature much plainer, buff-brown and olive; note bill shape and white undertail.

habitat.text: Extensive fresh wetlands with still or slow shallow water, dense marsh cover and floating vegetation such as lily pads.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Walks on lily pads, runs on open shorelines and clambers through marsh vegetation and waterside trees, flicking its short tail.
Nods its head as it swims; flies short distances with legs dangling.
Omnivorous: seeds, fruits and leaves plus insects, frogs, snails and fish; sometimes eggs and young of other birds.
Noisy: squawks, cackles and grunts.

resources.title: Red-breasted merganser
resources.description: Identify Red-breasted merganser, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Red-breasted merganser (Mergus serrator): Slim, crested, fish-eating duck with a thin bill. Male: grey sides, dark reddish breast, shaggy crest and a conspicuous white collar; less white than a male common merganser. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds across Alaska and northern Canada; winters mainly on coastal waters of the United States and southern Canada, from the Pacific and Atlantic coasts to Texas and Florida, with large migration concentrations on the Great Lakes (e.g. Lake Erie in late fall).

rangeSummary.value: Breeds across Alaska and northern Canada; winters mainly on coastal waters of the United States and southern Canada, from the Pacific and Atlantic coasts to Texas and Florida, with large migration concentrations on the Great Lakes (e.g. Lake Erie in late fall).

identification.text: Slim, crested, fish-eating duck with a thin bill.
Male: grey sides, dark reddish breast, shaggy crest and a conspicuous white collar; less white than a male common merganser.
Female: brown head with little contrast against a whitish throat, and no sharp contrast between brown neck and white chest.
Young common mergansers in summer can look very similar.
Compared with the common merganser: The common merganser winters mostly on fresh water; males are whiter, and females show sharp contrast between brown neck and white chest.

habitat.text: Breeds around lakes and rivers in the northern forest and north into the tundra, nesting on the ground in dense cover. Winters mostly on coastal bays, estuaries and open ocean, with a few on ice-free reservoirs and large rivers.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Dives and swims underwater for small fish; groups sometimes hunt cooperatively, driving fish into shallow water.
Migrating flocks fly in V-formations or lines; may migrate later in spring and earlier in fall than the common merganser.
Usually silent apart from croaks and grunts in courtship.

resources.title: Ross's goose
resources.description: Identify Ross's goose, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Ross's goose (Anser rossii): 21-25 in; small white goose, smaller than a Snow Goose. Short bill lacking the Snow Goose's black 'grinning patch', often with a bumpy blue-gray base. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Main population breeds in the central Canadian Arctic (Northwest Territories/Nunavut region) and migrates through Alberta and Montana to winter in central California; wintering numbers in New Mexico and east of the Rockies have increased markedly.

rangeSummary.value: Main population breeds in the central Canadian Arctic (Northwest Territories/Nunavut region) and migrates through Alberta and Montana to winter in central California; wintering numbers in New Mexico and east of the Rockies have increased markedly.

identification.text: 21-25 in; small white goose, smaller than a Snow Goose.
Short bill lacking the Snow Goose's black 'grinning patch', often with a bumpy blue-gray base.
Rounder head with the eye more centered, giving a gentle expression.
Young are much whiter than young Snow Geese; a rare blue morph exists.
Compared with the snow goose: Snow goose is larger with a longer bill showing a black 'grinning patch'; Ross's has a rounder head with a more centered eye.

habitat.text: Summer on flat Arctic tundra mixing grass and low dwarf birch or willow.
Migration and winter on shallow lakes, freshwater marshes and flooded stubble and other farm fields.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Migrates and winters in flocks, often mixed with Snow Geese; hybrids occur.
Feeds by walking, wading or swimming in shallow water; mainly green grasses and sedges, plus seeds and grain in fall.
Calls are soft cackling and grunting notes.

resources.title: Ruddy duck
resources.description: Identify Ruddy duck, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Ruddy duck (Oxyura jamaicensis): Stiff spiky tail often cocked upward. Male: dark cap and white cheeks; ruddy body and bright blue bill in breeding season. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds mainly on the northern prairies, from central British Columbia, southwestern Mackenzie and the Prairie Provinces east across southern Canada to Nova Scotia and south to California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas; northern breeders winter south to Central America.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds mainly on the northern prairies, from central British Columbia, southwestern Mackenzie and the Prairie Provinces east across southern Canada to Nova Scotia and south to California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas; northern breeders winter south to Central America.

identification.text: Stiff spiky tail often cocked upward.
Male: dark cap and white cheeks; ruddy body and bright blue bill in breeding season.
Female: pale cheeks crossed by a smeary dark line.
Wings solid dark in flight.

habitat.text: Breeds on fresh or alkaline lakes and ponds with marshy borders and open water; winters on sheltered shallow coastal bays and ice-free inland lakes.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Patters across the water to take off and seems reluctant to fly; almost helpless on land
Dives and strains food from bottom mud; insects and larvae are main summer foods
Usually silent; courting males make ticking and clapping sounds
Migrates mostly at night in small flocks

resources.title: Sora
resources.description: Identify Sora, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Sora (Porzana carolina): Chunky, short-billed rail, 20-25 cm. Adult: black face contrasting with a rich brown back, grey chest and a yellow bill. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds across much of Canada and the northern and western United States and winters in the southern United States and south to South America; recorded in every region from Alaska and the North to Florida.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds across much of Canada and the northern and western United States and winters in the southern United States and south to South America; recorded in every region from Alaska and the North to Florida.

identification.text: Chunky, short-billed rail, 20-25 cm.
Adult: black face contrasting with a rich brown back, grey chest and a yellow bill.
Juvenile: lacks the black face and is buffier below; sometimes mistaken for the rare yellow rail.
Compared with the virginia rail: The Virginia rail has a long bill and rusty-cinnamon underparts; the sora is short-billed with a yellow bill and black face.
Compared with the yellow rail: A juvenile sora lacks the black face and can suggest a yellow rail; check carefully.

habitat.text: Freshwater marshes with large stands of cattails, wet meadows and grassy pond edges; also salt marshes, especially in winter.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Heard far more than seen: a musical series of piping notes rapidly descending the scale, and a rising 'ker-wee'.
Large numbers may gather in marshes in late summer and early fall to fatten before migrating; migrates mostly at night, many to South America.
Picks food from the surface; eats many seeds of marsh plants (heavily on wild rice in late summer and fall), plus insects and snails.

resources.title: Surf scoter
resources.description: Identify Surf scoter, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Surf scoter (Melanitta perspicillata): Male all black with white head patches and an orange-and-white bill. Female dark sooty brown with two whitish patches on the face. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from western Alaska and the Mackenzie Delta across the northern Prairie Provinces to James Bay, Labrador and Newfoundland; winters on the Pacific coast from the Aleutians to Baja California and on the Atlantic from Nova Scotia to Florida, with some on the Great Lakes.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from western Alaska and the Mackenzie Delta across the northern Prairie Provinces to James Bay, Labrador and Newfoundland; winters on the Pacific coast from the Aleutians to Baja California and on the Atlantic from Nova Scotia to Florida, with some on the Great Lakes.

identification.text: Male all black with white head patches and an orange-and-white bill.
Female dark sooty brown with two whitish patches on the face.
Note the shape of the bill base at close range.

habitat.text: Breeds near lakes and slow rivers in sparse northern forest or tundra; winters mostly on shallow ocean bays and estuaries, some on the Great Lakes.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Springs forward to dive with wings partly opened; eats mainly mollusks
Silent most of the year
Migrates in flocks, flying high overland; inland lake stops are mostly for rest
Common in winter around Pacific piers and harbours

resources.title: Trumpeter swan
resources.description: Identify Trumpeter swan, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Trumpeter swan (Cygnus buccinator): Very large, all-white swan with a massive all-black bill. Lacks a yellow spot in front of the eye. Do not shoot unless you are certain of the species. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Alaska, northwestern Canada and the northwestern US, with reintroduced populations in the Great Lakes region including Ontario, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan and Ohio.

rangeSummary.value: Alaska, northwestern Canada and the northwestern US, with reintroduced populations in the Great Lakes region including Ontario, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan and Ohio.

identification.text: Very large, all-white swan with a massive all-black bill.
Lacks a yellow spot in front of the eye.
Immatures are darker than adults.
Compared with the tundra swan: Tundra swan is smaller, usually has a yellow spot before the eye and gives a higher call.

habitat.text: Large, shallow, vegetated freshwater ponds and wide, slow rivers; also lakes and winter bays.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Bugling ko-hoh call, lower than the tundra swan's.
Feeds on submerged plants by reaching or up-ending; occasionally feeds on land in winter.
Southern populations are mostly non-migratory; northern birds move south in late fall as water freezes, flying low in V formations.

conservationStatus.text: Taking trumpeter swans is illegal in Utah, although the federal swan framework allots Utah a quota.
Swans are protected by federal and state law and closed to harvest.

resources.title: Tundra swan
resources.description: Identify Tundra swan, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Tundra swan (Cygnus columbianus): Large all-white swan, 3 ft 11 in-4 ft 7 in. Black bill (not orange as in Mute Swan), usually with a small yellow spot in front of the eye. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds on Arctic tundra of Alaska and northern Canada and migrates long distances to winter on both coasts and interior waters of the United States.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds on Arctic tundra of Alaska and northern Canada and migrates long distances to winter on both coasts and interior waters of the United States.

identification.text: Large all-white swan, 3 ft 11 in-4 ft 7 in.
Black bill (not orange as in Mute Swan), usually with a small yellow spot in front of the eye.
Juveniles dull gray-brown with a pinkish bill, whitening by midwinter.
Call a mellow, bugling 'hoo-ho-hoo', often heard from migrating flocks.
Compared with the mute swan: Mute swan has an orange bill; adult tundra swan's bill is black, usually with a small yellow spot before the eye.

habitat.text: Breeds on northern tundra with many lakes and ponds, usually near the coast.
Winters on shallow lakes, wide slow rivers and coastal estuaries, especially near farm fields.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Migrating flocks of up to 100 or more are made up of family groups; fall migration uses long flights between traditional staging areas.
Dabbles, dips or up-ends in water for aquatic plants; on migration and in winter feeds heavily on waste corn, barley and soybeans in fields, sometimes on moonlit nights.

resources.title: Virginia rail
resources.description: Identify Virginia rail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Virginia rail (Rallus limicola): Medium-sized rail, 21-25 cm, with a long bill. Rich rusty-cinnamon underparts contrasting with grey cheeks. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds across southern Canada and much of the United States and winters in the southern United States and northern Mexico, some as far as Guatemala.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds across southern Canada and much of the United States and winters in the southern United States and northern Mexico, some as far as Guatemala.

identification.text: Medium-sized rail, 21-25 cm, with a long bill.
Rich rusty-cinnamon underparts contrasting with grey cheeks.
Sharp black-and-white bars on the flanks and reddish wings.
Juveniles are blackish at first.
Compared with the king rail: The king rail is much larger with tan or brownish rather than grey cheeks.
Compared with the sora: The sora is short-billed with a yellow bill and black face; the Virginia rail is long-billed with grey cheeks.

habitat.text: Fresh and brackish marshes for nesting, often in drier spots than the sora where both breed; moves into salt marshes in winter.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Seldom seen but often heard: a far-carrying 'ticket, ticket, ticket' and various grunts.
Probes mud and shallow water or stalks small prey; eats mostly aquatic insects and larvae, plus crayfish, snails and worms.
Most migrate to the southern United States and northern Mexico; some western U.S. populations may be resident.

resources.title: White-winged dove
resources.description: Identify White-winged dove, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: White-winged dove (Zenaida asiatica): Bulkier than a mourning dove, with a shorter tail; 28-32 cm. Big white wing patches, most obvious in flight. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mainly a summer resident in the southwestern United States (California to Texas), with year-round birds in Florida and along the Gulf Coast in winter; expanding northward, with strays far north of the breeding range.

rangeSummary.value: Mainly a summer resident in the southwestern United States (California to Texas), with year-round birds in Florida and along the Gulf Coast in winter; expanding northward, with strays far north of the breeding range.

identification.text: Bulkier than a mourning dove, with a shorter tail; 28-32 cm.
Big white wing patches, most obvious in flight.
White tips on the outer tail feathers.
Sexes similar.
Compared with the mourning dove: The white-winged dove is bulkier and shorter-tailed with large white wing patches.

habitat.text: Semi-open southwestern habitats: river woods, mesquite, saguaro desert, native Texas brushland, chaparral and open oak woods; adapts readily to farmland, suburbs and citrus groves.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Males give crowing calls on spring mornings from streamside groves and desert washes.
Early migrant: most arrive by March and leave in September; a few winter north of Mexico, mainly in towns; Florida birds are mostly resident.
Feeds on wild seeds, grain, acorns and fruit, especially cactus; often perches atop saguaros for fruit and nectar and is an important saguaro pollinator.
May nest in colonies in isolated groves surrounded by good feeding areas.

resources.title: White-winged scoter
resources.description: Identify White-winged scoter, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: White-winged scoter (Melanitta deglandi): Largest scoter. White wing patch, obvious in flight but often hidden on the water. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds across Alaska and Canada; winters on both coasts and the Great Lakes, with inland occurrences on large waters.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds across Alaska and Canada; winters on both coasts and the Great Lakes, with inland occurrences on large waters.

identification.text: Largest scoter.
White wing patch, obvious in flight but often hidden on the water.
Drake black with a small white teardrop around the eye.
Hens and immature males very dark with paler facial patches.
Compared with the surf scoter: Hens are told apart by differing face and eye pattern; white-winged shows the white wing patch.

habitat.text: Breeds on lakes, ponds and slow rivers in open country; winters on coastal salt bays and ocean shallows, especially over shellfish beds.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Flocks fly low in wavering lines over water.
Generally silent; soft whistles and guttural croaks.
Dives for mollusks, crustaceans, aquatic insects and some fish.
Males winter farther north than females and young.

resources.title: Whooping crane
resources.description: Identify Whooping crane, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Whooping crane (Grus americana): Very tall (4 ft 11 in-5 ft 3 in), mostly white crane with black wingtips shown in flight. Adult has bare red skin on the head and a dark facial pattern. Do not shoot unless you are certain of the species. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: One of the rarest North American birds; the wild migratory flock nests in Wood Buffalo National Park in central Canada and winters on the central Texas coast, about 2,400 miles away. It once nested more widely on the northern prairies.

rangeSummary.value: One of the rarest North American birds; the wild migratory flock nests in Wood Buffalo National Park in central Canada and winters on the central Texas coast, about 2,400 miles away. It once nested more widely on the northern prairies.

identification.text: Very tall (4 ft 11 in-5 ft 3 in), mostly white crane with black wingtips shown in flight.
Adult has bare red skin on the head and a dark facial pattern.
Juvenile has brown on the head and back.
Trumpet-like call carries for several miles.
Compared with the wood stork: Compare the black wing pattern in flight; the whooping crane is a different shape and has a red-and-dark head pattern.
Compared with the american white pelican: Also white with black in the wings; compare shape and the crane's long legs and red crown.

habitat.text: Breeds in remote muskeg (swampy coniferous forest with many ponds); winters in coastal marsh.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Migrates by day in family groups or small flocks along narrow corridors with traditional stopovers.
Wintering pairs and families defend feeding territories, returning to the same territory each winter.
Omnivorous; in winter eats crabs, clams, shrimp, insects, frogs, fish, acorns and berries.

conservationStatus.text: Listed as Endangered on Schedule 1 of the Species at Risk Act.
The whooping crane, Wherever found, except where listed as an experimental population: listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.

blocks.title: If you are not certain, do not shoot

content.plainText: Swans are hard to tell apart at hunting distance, and a missing yellow spot is not proof. Where a swan season is open, confirm the species before you shoot; if you are not certain, do not shoot.

blocks.title: If you are not certain, do not shoot

content.plainText: Whooping cranes migrate through the same prairie country and at the same time of year as sandhill cranes, often in mixed flocks. Identify every bird before you shoot: at dawn, in fog or against the sky, colour can be hard to read. If any bird in a flock could be a whooping crane, do not shoot.
Whooping crane is listed as Endangered on Schedule 1 of Canada's Species at Risk Act and is protected under the Migratory Birds Convention Act, 1994.
